newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister backs down on anti-Clinton charge.
newsitem.headline: French minister backs down on anti-Clinton charge.

text.p: A French cabinet minister who sparked a row with Washington after questioning the motives of U.S. Africa policy refused on Wednesday to withdraw his remarks but later sought to end the row.

The row began when junior cooperation minister Jacques Godfrain told reporters last week that an African tour by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher was aimed at promoting President Bill Clinton's re-election.

"I'm not retracting what I said. Nowhere have I said anything which was not true," Godfrain initially told reporters on Wednesday in response to a demand by the U.S. State Department that he withdraw his remarks.
State Department Nicholas Burns said Godfrain's statement last week was "a ludicrous charge made by someone who's not paid attention to what the United States has done".
U.S. officials had said France was upset by Christopher's trip because they saw it as trespassing on a French domain.

Godfrain insisted earlier on Wednesday: "I said that U.S. aid to Africa is declining and it is. I said President Clinton never went to Africa and he didn't. I said that Clinton never pronounced the word Africa at the United Nations and he never did."
"I also said we are just days away from the American election," said Godfrain, adding an African folk saying that "the truth does not blind but sometimes it prevents from seeing."
But several hours after his latest statements were broadcast, Godfrain's office issued a statement saying the minister "was astonished at the interpretation given to his words".
"He rejoiced at the visit to Africa of Mr Christopher and of the will of the United States to reinforce its action in favour of development," the statement said.

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt had earlier said on Wednesday that Foreign Minister Herve de Charette respected Christopher as "his colleague and friend...and we ourselves have the highest appreciation for the international role of the United States".
"We consider this affair closed," Rummelhardt added.
